name: Bianca Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the tablet compression suite at Verity Pharma, where we make generic blood-pressure and diabetes tablets. I start at 7, review the batch record, set up the press with the right tooling, and run weight, hardness and thickness checks every half hour. It's very clean, very regulated work, and one wrong signature can sink a whole batch.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the precision and the fact that what I do ends up in somebody's medicine cabinet. What wears me out is the paperwork, honestly, every step has to be recorded and double-checked, and the gowning up in the suite four or five times a day. Plus I'm on my feet for most of the shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, it's a useful tool and that's it. I'd tell the team to use it for the parts that don't touch the regulated records, like drafting a troubleshooting note or summarising a long procedure. Online I'd stay out of it, because the hype crowd is tiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be a bit relieved, because my retirement plan stays on track. I'm 58, I'd like to work another four years, and a slow AI world means my job and my plant stay as they are. Still, I'm a person who likes change, so I'd feel a little bored.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running the press and keep using AI for first drafts of deviation reports and for reading the vendor's service manuals. I'd put 250 a month into the pension top-up, and I'd take the validation course my manager keeps suggesting. It would open a quieter job for my last few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, balanced. Not excited, not scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day already. What does it do for you in a regulated plant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The assistant writes the first draft of a deviation report from my bullet points, and I fix the facts. It also helps me read the service manuals for the press and spot patterns in the rejects. It never touches the batch record itself, because that has to be by a person with a signature.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How are things at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We're fine. My partner Hugo is an electrician and works for himself, so his income goes up and down, but we've kept four months of savings. Our son Mateo is a paramedic and our daughter Lucia is finishing teacher training, so they need little from us.

Online I'd stay out of it, because the **hype crowd** is tiring.
think: A slow AI world keeps my plant and my **retirement plan** on track.
I like change, so I'd feel a little **bored**.
do: Keep running the press and using AI for **first drafts** of deviation reports.
Put **250 a month** into the pension top-up.
Take the **validation course** my manager keeps suggesting.

steps.text: Keep drafting deviation reports with AI and fixing the facts myself
Put 250 a month into the pension top-up
Take the validation course for a quieter final job
Keep running the compression press until retirement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the likeliest picture and I'm quite pleased to be ready. At work I'd run a short session for the crew on how to use the assistant safely. And I'd tell management not to treat it as a way to cut heads, because we need the knowledge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job gets safer if I'm smart. The reviewing, scheduling and report writing go to software, but a person still has to sign and stand behind a medicine. Robots will come into the packaging halls first, and the press suite, with its clean-room rules, a bit later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the plant's automation and data course, and I'd ask to be the operator who helps validate the new software. I'd aim to become the person who checks what the AI produced, which a regulator will insist on. And I'd put another few hundred into the pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Interested. There's some nerves in it, but they're the good kind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which tasks in your own job are thinking tasks that software takes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Batch record review, scheduling, change-control paperwork and the first read of any lab data. Quite a lot of the office and quality teams would shrink or change. I'd say a third of those tasks could be done by software within two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your plant do differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd probably automate the packaging line first, since it's the easy bit, and put cameras on the presses. The company would say it's to reduce errors, and that's partly true. I'd tell my manager to keep a few senior people on the floor who understand the product.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we must get serious today. I'd call a meeting at the plant and say I'm willing to help plan the changes, because the plant can't do this alone. Two years is short, and regulators don't move fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be worried, and I'd also be calculating. The reviewing and report work goes in 2028, and my quality colleagues might be cut by half. I have about three years more on the press before robots take it, and with only four months of savings, I'm not sure that's enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd talk with Hugo and cut spending by a quarter. I'd throw myself into the plant's automation project and offer to be the lead operator on the first robot-fed press. I'd also ask the pension fund what it would cost to retire at 61 and build a spreadsheet of my options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and wired. Part of me wants to roll up my sleeves, part of me wants to hide under the bed covers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The robots come around 2031. How does your hands-on work fit with that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pharma is a tight regulatory field, so robots will come slower than in other factories because every change needs validation. That might give me a few extra months. But I wouldn't bet my pension on it, because the company could still decide to replace the press crew with a robot line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your children that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my son Mateo that people in emergencies still need people, so he's fine. And my daughter Lucia, who's training to be a teacher, should learn how to use the AI as a classroom tool. I'd tell them both not to panic, because their mum has a plan, a rough one.

say: I'd say we must **get serious today**, and I'd offer to help the plant plan.
Regulators don't move fast, but two years is **short**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a good chance if we do the work, and I'd say it loudly at the plant. Five years is enough to retrain a whole crew. I'd tell people that the ones who learn early will have the pick of the new jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quietly, I think I'd be all right. AI arrives when I'm 63 and the robots when I'm 66, so I could be a trained technician by then or retired. My worry is for the younger operators and the quality staff, who'd face it with half the savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first year on the automation and validation courses, and I'd ask the plant to give me a place on the first robot project. I'd save 400 a month, so I'd have about nine months in the bank. And I'd talk to Hugo about whether his one-man business should hire an apprentice, since it's good work for a young person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful. I like a deadline that gives you room to run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years gives you more time. What would you do with it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pharma will always need people who understand both the machine and the regulation, so I'd retrain as an automation technician at the technical college. That would be night classes for two years, and it would pay a little more too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly Karim, who's 29 and runs the capsule line. He's great at the work, but he avoids anything with a screen. I'd sit him down and teach him the assistant over a coffee, because a few hours now could save him later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the version where we get to do this properly. I'd tell my plant that ten years is enough to design new jobs, not just cut old ones. And I'd say it publicly, because the plants that plan now will keep the best people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's calm. I'd be retired before robots reach my kind of work in 2039, so my own risk is small. I'd just want to see my kids settle, and for the pension and healthcare systems to still work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work until around 62, then go part-time as a trainer or auditor if the plant wants me. I'd keep using the AI tools and pass what I know to younger staff. And I'd put money into a small index fund, since I'd have time and spare cash after the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a little excited. I'd like to see what a pharma plant looks like then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is long. Would you change anything about how you plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, and I'd keep my plan. I'd just stay curious, and keep a six-month cushion. I think the people who do well are the ones who keep learning a bit every year, not only when there's a scare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell somebody starting in pharma now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say pick a place where machines and rules both matter, like pharma or food, and learn the machine and the paperwork together. And I'd say that good judgment is the rarest thing in any plant, so build it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because regulators and plants don't change in that time. What would help is paid training hours, a clear pension route for people over 55, and honest numbers from the company about what's planned.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about trust. A tablet is only worth something if somebody stands behind it. I'd want a person to stay responsible for every batch, however clever the software is.

headlineQuote: A tablet is only worth something
portrait: **Bianca** is a 58-year-old tablet press operator at a generic drug plant, planning to work another four years.
She uses **AI every day** for drafts and manuals, but never on signed batch records.
Her partner is self-employed, so she keeps about **four months** of savings and cuts spending when needed.
She is calm in four pictures and turns **uneasy** only in the two-year world, where plant and regulator can't keep up.
biggestWorry: The **two-year scenario**, because regulators and plants can't change in that time.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training hours**, a clear pension route for over-55s and honest numbers from the company about its plans.
